questions.explain: The pragmatic answer: migration-based for production where explicit control over exactly what runs matters (e.g., avoiding an unapproved table rebuild), state-based for dev environments where speed matters.
options: Migration-based for production, state-based for development
State-based for production, migration-based for development
State-based everywhere; migrations are obsolete
Manual scripts in production, pipelines in dev
questions.q: When should you use migration-based versus state-based database deployments?

questions.explain: The Test stage deploys migrations to an ephemeral database (container per PR or serverless copy) and runs tSQLt tests, data-migration validation, and Query Store performance regression checks.
options: Running migrations directly on staging
Peer review of the SQL files only
Deploying to an ephemeral database and running tSQLt tests plus Query Store regression checks
Restoring production to a developer laptop
questions.q: What does the Test stage of a SQL Server CI/CD pipeline do?

questions.explain: Expand/contract deploys in phases — add the new column/table alongside the old (expand), migrate the application, then remove the old (contract) — so the database is never incompatible with the running app.
options: Deploying the app and database simultaneously
Renaming the table while the app is running
Running down-migrations first
Adding the new schema element alongside the old, migrating the app, then removing the old
questions.q: What is the expand/contract (parallel change) pattern for breaking schema changes?

questions.explain: The honest strategies are roll forward (fix with a new migration), restore (point-in-time, accepting data loss), and expand/contract discipline; down-migrations are rarely tested and often wrong.
options: Always rely on tested down-migrations
Roll forward with a new migration, restore for data-corrupting failures, or design with expand/contract so rollback is rarely needed
Restore the previous night's tape backup
Re-run the migration with different parameters
questions.q: What is the chapter's honest guidance on database rollback?

questions.explain: Non-production environments must never hold real customer data; use dynamic data masking, static masking, or synthetic data so a compromised dev environment is an embarrassment, not a breach notification.
options: Restoring full production backups to dev for realism
Anonymizing data by deleting half the rows
Never holding real customer data in non-production; using masking or synthetic generation instead
Trusting developers not to copy data out
questions.q: What is the rule for production data in non-production environments?
